content: When required by national regulations, a technique involving a lance attached to a hand compression sprayer is used for indoor residual spraying. This method produces significantly larger spray droplets compared to cold fogging applications. Aero-Sense, a company based in Belgium, has faced similar challenges as its competitors but noted that Europe offers a favorable market for producers. Once a product completes the often stringent registration process, it can be sold across all EU countries. Concerns were raised about the potential need for pesticide application at airport entrances, emphasizing that other modes of transport, such as trucks and container ships, also contribute to the international spread of disease vectors. British Airways is responsible for ensuring disinsection compliance on its aircraft, unlike in some countries where local health authorities handle this responsibility. Noncompliance may stem from overly detailed requirements, and simplifying regulations could improve adherence. It was also noted that buses transporting passengers to aircraft, as well as vehicles delivering luggage, can carry disease vectors. E-Mist Innovations Inc. has developed an electrostatic insecticide application method that allows for rapid disinsection of surfaces. The company is working on a handheld, battery-powered device for disinfecting aircraft cabins and has created a battery-powered backpack for electrostatic disinsection of cargo holds. They have collaborated with the U.S. Department of Defense and claim success in creating barriers against insects in large spaces. Their products have been used to reduce infections in schools and hospitals. However, the cost of aircraft disinsection equipment is likely higher than current methods, though the application cost is significantly lower than chemical methods. The electrostatic method is primarily used for treating luggage and cargo holds with residual spray but is not applied in cabins. A smaller version of the device may be suitable for pre-embarkation treatment. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) has been tasked with working alongside the World Health Organization (WHO) to review disinsection recommendations and explore non-chemical disinsection options. ICAO has also established an Airport Vector Control Register to maintain a 400-meter perimeter around airports free of disease vectors. ICAO is working to harmonize standards and has stressed the need for guidelines on vector surveillance and control at airports. Non-chemical disinsection methods, such as air curtains at aircraft doors, are being investigated to prevent mosquito entry. However, no entity is ready to invest in standard operating procedures until WHO provides recommendations on non-chemical disinsection. WHO has been asked to establish standards and performance criteria for non-chemical methods, aiming for 90% vector control. Other proposed methods include ultraviolet scanning, sonic devices, and insect repellents that exclude insects rather than kill them. ICAO is also considering a risk assessment model for aircraft traveling between airports, focusing on vectors of concern and seasonal variations. Challenges arise when aircraft make unscheduled stopovers, raising political and operational concerns. As climate patterns change, the risk of disease vectors will also evolve. While the proposed risk model was appreciated, maintaining its accuracy over time may be challenging due to a lack of baseline data. The idea of placing mosquito traps in aircraft cabins was discussed to assess the extent of disease vector transportation via passenger aircraft. However, this method may not capture mosquitoes in cargo holds. While non-chemical disinsection is preferred, its feasibility and effectiveness remain uncertain. WHO guidelines on disinsection are outdated, and updated recommendations are urgently needed. The International Health Regulations (IHR) recommend that airport buildings and conveyances be free of infection sources, including vectors. Effective vector control within a 400-meter perimeter of international airports is necessary, considering the active flight range of mosquitoes. ICAO has emphasized the need for improved vector control at airports and on departing aircraft. Air curtains, already used in some public spaces, have shown promise but face challenges in ensuring 100% effectiveness due to variations in aircraft shapes. Further investigation is needed to assess the viability of fitting air curtains during aircraft manufacturing. The responsibility for disinsection varies, with some airports handling it, while in other cases, airlines or local health authorities are responsible. WHO has focused on preventing mosquito transmission but also considers other pests like mites, ticks, bed bugs, and rodents. Various disinsection methods, including pre-embarkation, pre-flight, and top-of-descent spraying, have been evaluated. Each method has advantages and limitations, with compliance and proper application being critical for effectiveness. Residual spraying, while effective, can lead to operational complexities and passenger complaints due to excessive wetting and stickiness. Updated WHO guidelines are needed to address these challenges and provide clear recommendations for effective and safe disinsection practices.
